summariesJSON.title: Page 1
summariesJSON.content: This page introduces key pre-Socratic philosophers and their ideas. Thales of Miletus, from around 624-546 BCE, proposed water as the fundamental substance and believed everything is made of water, the earth floats on it, and all things are full of gods (animism). Anaximander, a student of Thales, lived circa 610-546 BCE and suggested the 'apeiron' (the infinite) as a primary principle, first mapped the known world, and proposed an early theory of evolution. Heraclitus, from approximately 535-475 BCE, emphasized change with the famous statement "You cannot step into the same river twice," regarded fire as the core element, and developed concepts like the unity of opposites and logos (cosmic reason/order). In contrast, Parmenides (circa 515-450 BCE) argued change is an illusion; reality is static and unchanging, believing "Being is; non-being is not" and differentiating between the Way of Truth and the Way of Opinion.

summariesJSON.title: Document summary
summariesJSON.content: This document presents an overview of key pre-Socratic philosophers, highlighting their core ideas and philosophies. Thales of Miletus proposed water as the fundamental substance of the universe and introduced early concepts of animism. His student, Anaximander, introduced the concept of the 'apeiron' (the infinite), mapped the known world, and proposed preliminary evolutionary theories. Heraclitus emphasized perpetual change and introduced the concepts of the unity of opposites and logos, considering fire as the primary element. The contrasting philosophy of Parmenides posited that change is an illusion, asserting that reality is static and that 'Being' alone truly exists. These foundational ideas significantly influenced the trajectory of Western philosophical thought.
